title: Serbia's emission reduction plan fails as EPS coal plants breach ceilings
programme: National Emission Reduction Plan (NERP) under the Large Combustion Plants Directive
problem: Serbia's ageing EPS lignite plants emit far more sulphur dioxide, dust and nitrogen oxides than the Large Combustion Plants Directive allows.
solution: Instead of plant-by-plant limits from 2018, Serbia adopted a NERP with national emission ceilings that tighten until 2027, relying on EPS desulphurisation and other pollution-control investments.
implementer: Government of Serbia (Ministry for Environmental Protection)
funding: EPS's own investment budget; its 2025-2027 business plan adds EUR 100 million for pollution control.
results: In 2025 Serbia's NERP coal plants emitted 177,756 tonnes of SO2, 5.1 times the ceiling, and breached all three pollutant ceilings for the first time; Kostolac B, despite its desulphurisation unit, still emitted 3.3 times its ceiling.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own compliance record under the Energy Community Treaty, for plants run by state-owned EPS. The Energy Community Secretariat escalated its case in July 2025, and continued breaches weaken Serbia's position now that CBAM charges apply to electricity exports.
adapt_needed: Cut operating hours at non-compliant units until pollution controls work, and set closure dates where retrofits are not viable.
blockers: Authorities have never fined EPS for these breaches, and a draft IPPC law appears permissive towards plants operating without permits.
quote: In spite of a visible decline in the last three years, SO 2 emissions from the NERP coal power plants in Serbia were still over 5 times above the national ceiling in 2025, up from 4.6 times in 2024, as the ceiling is decreasing annually.

title: Nikola Tesla A desulphurisation cuts SO2 but still misses ceiling
programme: Flue gas desulphurisation at Nikola Tesla A3-A6
problem: Nikola Tesla A, one of EPS's largest lignite plants, emitted far more sulphur dioxide than its NERP ceiling allowed.
solution: EPS installed a desulphurisation unit on units A3-A6, which was commissioned in 2024 after a trial run.
results: SO2 emissions fell from nearly 60,000 tonnes in 2023 to almost 21,000 in 2025 but stayed at twice the plant's individual ceiling; the unit was commissioned 13 years after funding was secured.
serbia_reason: This is EPS's own flagship pollution-control investment, made to meet Serbia's NERP obligations under the Energy Community Treaty. It shows large retrofits can cut emissions but arrive late and still fall short of legal limits.
adapt_needed: Future EPS retrofits need performance guarantees tied to legal ceilings and real-time public emissions data.
blockers: Retrofits are costly and energy-consuming, making old plants less efficient just as CBAM makes coal power less competitive.
quote: Despite a considerable reduction of SO 2 emissions from nearly 60,000 tonnes in 2023 to almost 21,000 in 2025, this amount is still twice as much sulphur dioxide as the plant's individual ceiling in 2025. This cannot count as good value for money by any stretch of the imagination.

title: Serbia keeps opt-out Morava and Kolubara A coal plants running illegally
programme: LCPD opt-out (limited lifetime derogation) for Morava and Kolubara A
problem: Serbia's oldest EPS lignite units, Morava and Kolubara A, could not meet EU pollution limits without major retrofits.
solution: Serbia placed them under the opt-out derogation, allowing up to 20,000 operating hours between 2018 and 2023 before closure; EPS announced closure for end-2024 and tendered conservation and decommissioning studies.
results: Morava ran another 2,875 hours in 2025 although its hours expired at the end of 2022, and Kolubara A5 ran 2,200 hours; the closure date slipped to 'by 2030', and the Energy Community Secretariat issued a reasoned opinion in March 2026.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own case, run by state-owned EPS under the Large Combustion Plants Directive of the Energy Community Treaty. Missed closure deadlines have led to dispute settlement and undermine the credibility of Serbia's coal phase-out plans.
adapt_needed: Set binding unit-by-unit closure dates linked to replacement capacity, such as the planned solar plants on the Kolubara and Morava ash dumps.
blockers: Energy security arguments and the strategy's 'by 2030' wording give EPS room to keep the units running.
quote: Serbia kept its antiquated Morava power plant running for another illegal 2,875 hours in 2025, in breach of the 'opt-out' derogation, as its allotted operating hours had already expired at the end of 2022.

title: Serbia's low carbon tax is a weak tool for coal phase-out
programme: Carbon tax and domestic CBAM law (2025)
problem: Serbia's coal-heavy power sector pays no meaningful carbon price while the EU's CBAM now charges carbon-intensive imports, including electricity.
solution: In late 2025 Serbia introduced a carbon tax and its own reverse version of CBAM, taxing carbon-intensive imports.
results: The tax is only four euros per tonne with no sign of increases, the CBAM law does not cover electricity, and the law does not guarantee that revenues go to the energy transition.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own first step on carbon pricing, taken in response to EU CBAM exposure. Without a rising price and earmarked revenues it is unlikely to shift EPS away from lignite.
adapt_needed: Set a rising price path towards EU ETS levels, cover the power sector and earmark revenues for the energy transition.
blockers: Fear of higher electricity prices and EPS's dependence on lignite make a meaningful carbon price politically hard.
quote: However, the CBAM law does not apply to the electricity sector, and the legislation on carbon pricing sets a tax of only four euros per tonne, with no indication that it will increase in the future. The system is so full of loopholes, rebates and subsidies that it can at best be considered a practice run in advance of the introduction of a more effective system.

title: Ugljevik's EUR 85 million desulphurisation unit sits unused as 'economic burden'
programme: Flue gas desulphurisation at Ugljevik power plant
problem: The Ugljevik lignite plant in Republika Srpska is the region's largest single sulphur dioxide emitter.
solution: A desulphurisation unit was installed at the plant and received an operating permit in November 2021.
results: Ugljevik emitted 115,079 tonnes of SO2 in 2025, 16.3 times its ceiling and its highest level since 2018, with emissions rising each year since 2022.
serbia_reason: EPS has similar desulphurisation units at Kostolac B and Nikola Tesla. Ugljevik shows that without enforcement of Energy Community pollution rules, a state utility may leave costly equipment idle to save operating costs.
adapt_needed: Make operating permits conditional on continuous, real-time monitoring that proves pollution controls are running.
blockers: No Western Balkan authority has fined a plant operator for these breaches, so utilities pay nothing for idling equipment.
quote: Its operator admits that the de-SO X is not working mainly because it is an 'economic burden', and it looks increasingly doubtful that this EUR 85 million project will ever be properly used.

title: Kosova B retrofit stalls despite EUR 76.4 million IPA II grant
programme: Kosova B1 and B2 rehabilitation for Industrial Emissions Directive compliance (IPA II)
problem: Kosovo's Kosova B lignite units emit dust and nitrogen oxides far above their NERP ceilings.
solution: Kosovo planned to retrofit unit B1 by 2021 and B2 by 2022 to meet Industrial Emissions Directive limits, using an EU IPA II grant signed in November 2019 and budget allocations under its Energy Strategy.
implementer: Kosovo Ministry of Energy and Kosovo Energy Corporation (KEK)
funding: EU IPA II grant, plus allocations of EUR 88 million in 2024 and EUR 88 million in 2025 under the Energy Strategy.
results: The Ministry of Energy reports zero progress despite the 2024 and 2025 allocations; compliance dates slipped to October 2026 (B1) and October 2027 (B2), and Kosova B1 emitted 6.2 times its dust ceiling in 2025.
serbia_reason: Serbia also relies on EU pre-accession funds and its state utility to bring lignite units into line with Energy Community emission rules. Kosovo shows that a signed grant alone does not deliver retrofits when works are repeatedly delayed.
adapt_needed: Attach milestones and clawback conditions to IPA-funded retrofits and publish progress reports.
blockers: WBIF's Reform and Growth Facility does not allow support for fossil fuels, limiting new EU grant funding for coal retrofits.
quote: It envisaged that unit B2 would follow suit and comply by 2022, with the use of a EUR 76.4 million grant under the European Commission's Instrument for Pre-Accession II (IPA II) signed in November 2019. These works have been repeatedly and unjustifiably delayed.

title: Pljevlja retrofit after illegal opt-out operation leaves compliance uncertain
programme: Pljevlja ecological reconstruction (retrofit) after the LCPD opt-out
problem: Montenegro's only coal plant, Pljevlja, used up its 20,000 opt-out operating hours by late 2020 but kept running.
solution: State utility EPCG kept the plant operating and contracted a retrofit in 2020 to meet EU best-available-technique standards, taking the plant offline in 2025 for the main works.
results: After restarting in November 2025, very high nitrogen oxide and sulphur dioxide levels were measured in Pljevlja and the plant's automatic measuring equipment was not working; denitrification began in January 2026 and desulphurisation entered trial operation in February 2026, with results not yet known.
serbia_reason: Like EPS's Morava and Kolubara A, Pljevlja is a state-utility unit that overran its opt-out hours under the Energy Community Treaty. It shows the legal and cost risks of retrofitting an old unit instead of closing it.
adapt_needed: Serbia should weigh any life-extension retrofit against closure, carbon pricing and CBAM costs before signing contracts.
blockers: Plants seen as vital for supply security create pressure to extend their life rather than close them.
quote: Overall, the end of the main retrofit works has brought more questions than answers, and it remains to be seen whether Pljevlja will ever be able to meet EU pollution control standards.

title: North Macedonia's coal phase-out plans undercut by utility's new lignite mine
programme: Just Transition Roadmap and NECP coal phase-out by 2030
problem: North Macedonia's old lignite plants breach their NERP ceilings, while planned closure dates keep slipping.
solution: The government adopted a Just Transition Roadmap (2023), an Accelerating Coal Transition Investment Plan (2024) and an updated NECP with a 2030 coal phase-out scenario, leaving the unit closure timeline to state utility AD ESM.
results: Oslomej's closure has been pushed from 2019 to the end of 2026 and it still operated in 2025, while an EIA for the new Zhivojno lignite mine was approved in September 2025; private investors drive a significant increase in solar and wind generation.
serbia_reason: North Macedonia is the region's most advanced planner for a just transition, with a state utility similar to EPS. It shows that plans made in the Energy Community NECP process fail if the state utility keeps investing in new coal.
adapt_needed: Serbia's NECP update would need unit-level closure dates that bind EPS rather than leaving them to the utility.
blockers: A state utility's interest in protecting coal assets and jobs can override national transition plans.
quote: On paper, the country has reaffirmed its commitment to phase out coal power generation in its updated NECP. However, the actions of the government and AD ESM are not aligned with strategic documents.
